extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets and educated young Romans (writers and students of literature)
extracted.subtask_description: Epistolary poetic instruction and moral advice for poets and young men about study, conduct, and the habits that make a good writer/person. Emphasises what to read, when to learn, self-discipline, moderation, and independence of mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect wisdom for future use
rubrics_metrics.description: I search and search, and when I find, I lay The wisdom up against a rainy day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively seek out useful knowledge and 'lay it up' so it can be applied when needed later; treat wisdom as a reserve for hard times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: I've taken no man's shilling; none Of all your fathers owns me for his son; Just where the weather drives me, I invite Myself to take up quarters for the night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt a sect or merely follow fashions for pay or favour; cultivate independent thinking rather than becoming someone's client or partisan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin study where you can
rubrics_metrics.description: Well, if I cannot be a student, yet There's good in spelling at the alphabet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If advanced study is impossible, begin with the basics — even small efforts at learning and practice matter and accumulate over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate yourself patiently
rubrics_metrics.description: Run through the list of faults; whate'er you be, ... Submit to culture patiently, you'll find Her charms can humanize the rudest mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patient self-cultivation and education can improve character and manner; deliberate refinement is recommended for any writer or person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vice; aim for progressive moral improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: To fly from vice is virtue: to be free From foolishness is wisdom's first degree. Some point of moral progress each may gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral progress — avoiding vice and folly — is foundational; small attainable improvements are valuable and expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer exemplars who show what helps and harms
rubrics_metrics.description: What's good, what's bad, what helps, what hurts, he shows Better in verse than Crantor does in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study exemplary poets (here, Homer) because narrative poetry can vividly teach consequences of passion and action; learn from great models to understand human motives and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from stories of wisdom and folly (use examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn to the second tale: Ulysses shows How worth and wisdom triumph over woes: ... The Sirens' song you know, and Circe's bowl ... Had that sweet draught seduced his stupid soul ... he had been The senseless chattel of a wanton queen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exempla — tales of heroes and their choices — to learn how wisdom triumphs and how pleasure can lead to ruin; narratives are teaching tools for writers and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not procrastinate — begin learning and acting now
rubrics_metrics.description: Come now, have courage to be wise: begin: You're halfway over when you once plunge in: He who puts off the time for mending, stands A clodpoll by the stream with folded hands, Waiting till all the water be gone past; But it runs on, and will, while time shall last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate action is crucial: starting is the major step toward improvement — delay wastes opportunity; this applies to study, composition, and moral correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read wholesome books to form high resolves
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless you light your lamp ere dawn and read Some wholesome book that high resolves may breed, You'll find your sleep go from you, and will toss Upon your pillow, envious, lovesick, cross.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular reading of morally and intellectually nourishing works cultivates resolve and steadiness of mind; literature should be part of daily discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set limits on desires — practice moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Make light of pleasure: pleasure bought with pain Yields little profit, but much more of bane. The miser's always needy: draw a line Within whose bound your wishes to confine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate pleasures and control desires; for a stable life and clear writing/mind set boundaries to appetite and ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control anger and passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Who governs not his wrath will wish undone The deeds he did 'when the rash mood was on.' Wrath is a short-lived madness: curb and bit Your mind: 'twill rule you, if you rule not it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional self-control is necessary; impulsive passions lead to regrettable actions — vital for both personal conduct and clear, reasoned composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate early; take on wise mentors
rubrics_metrics.description: While the colt's mouth is soft, the trainer's skill Moulds it to follow at the rider's will. Now, while your system's plastic, ope each pore; Now seek wise friends, and drink in all their lore: The smell that's first imparted will adhere To seasoned jars through many an after year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formative impressions and early instruction are lasting; young writers should seek good teachers and absorb sound influences early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent; avoid inconstancy and caprice
rubrics_metrics.description: How, if my mind's inconsequent, rejects What late it longed for, what it loathed affects, Shifts every moment, with itself at strife, And makes a chaos of an ordered life, Builds castles up, then pulls them to the ground, Keeps changing round for square and square for round?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid capricious changes of purpose and taste; consistency of mind and plan leads to ordered work and life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simple moral instruction over cynical expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: Which is the better teacher, tell me, pray, The law of Roscius, or the children's lay That crowns fair dealing ... 'Make money, money, man; Well, if so be,--if not, which way you can,'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple moral teachings (like children's rhymes that praise fair dealing) can be better guides than sophisticated maxims that promote profit at any cost; prefer ethical clarity in shaping character and work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live within means; let wealth be servant not master
rubrics_metrics.description: Means should, like shoes, be neither large nor small; Too wide, they trip us up, too strait, they gall. Live contented ... Gold will be slave or master: 'tis more fit That it be led by us than we by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise moderation in material aims: contentment and fitting means to needs produces steadiness useful to creative work; do not allow pursuit of money to dominate life or art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a life suited to temperament (country vs city)
rubrics_metrics.description: You keep the nest: I love the country, Fresh runnels, moss-grown rocks, and woodland green. ... Drive Nature forth by force, she'll turn and rout The false refinements that would keep her out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an environment and lifestyle fitting your nature; authentic living supports authentic writing — do not adopt false refinements that contradict your temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opportunities and resources reasonably
rubrics_metrics.description: Why should the Gods have put me at my ease, If I mayn't use my fortune as I please? The man who stints and pinches for his heir Is next-door neighbour to a fool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in comfortable circumstances, use them reasonably (hospitality, conversation, study); don't hoard life for an uncertain future to the detriment of present flourishing and creative practice.
